title: REST Resources and HTTP Semantics
oneLiner: Nouns in the URL, verbs in the method, outcomes in the status code: what each HTTP method promises and why retries depend on it.
keyTakeaway: Model the API as resources (nouns such as /orders/42) and let the HTTP method say what happens to them. GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are safe (they change nothing); GET, PUT and DELETE are also idempotent (doing them twice leaves the same state as doing them once), which is what lets clients, proxies and load balancers retry them. POST and PATCH are neither, so a retried POST can create a second order unless the API adds an idempotency key. Return the status code that matches the outcome: 201 with a Location header for a create, 4xx when the client must change the request, 5xx when retrying later might work.
explanation:
An API (application programming interface) is the contract one program offers another: which requests it accepts, what it returns, and what it promises about each. Most public web APIs follow REST (representational state transfer), a style Roy Fielding described in his 2000 dissertation. The parts that matter in practice are few. The API is a set of resources, each with a URL: /users/7, /users/7/orders, /orders/42. A client works with a representation of a resource, usually a JSON document, and acts on it with the small fixed set of HTTP methods. Each request carries everything the server needs to handle it (the server keeps no per-client session between requests), which is what lets any server behind a load balancer answer any request.

Resource modelling comes first. URLs name things, not actions: POST /orders rather than POST /createOrder, and DELETE /orders/42 rather than GET /deleteOrder?id=42. Use plural collection names, put the id of one item after the collection, and nest only to show real ownership, one level deep: /users/7/orders is fine, /users/7/orders/42/items/3/options is a sign the item should be its own top-level resource. Some operations are genuinely verbs (cancel an order, send a password reset). Model them as a state change (PATCH /orders/42 with {"status": "cancelled"}), as a new resource (POST /orders/42/cancellations, which also gives you a record of who cancelled and why), or, as Google's API guidelines allow, as a custom method such as POST /orders/42:cancel. Filtering, sorting and paging go in the query string of a collection GET: /orders?status=open&sort=-created_at&limit=20.

Each method makes promises, and the rest of the web relies on them. A safe method (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) is read-only: crawlers, link prefetchers and caches call it freely, so a GET that deletes something will eventually be triggered by accident. An idempotent method has the same effect on the server whether it arrives once or five times. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent: PUT /users/7/email with a value replaces the whole email field, so repeating it changes nothing more; DELETE /orders/42 twice leaves the order deleted (the second call may answer 404, but the state is the same). POST is not idempotent: each POST /orders creates another order. PATCH (a partial update) is idempotent only if its body sets values rather than changing them relative to the current ones: {"quantity": 3} is safe to repeat, {"op": "increment"} is not. Idempotency is what makes retries safe. When a connection drops after the request was sent, the client cannot know whether the server acted, and HTTP libraries, proxies and service meshes automatically retry only the idempotent methods for exactly that reason. The Idempotency Keys lesson in this track fixes POST.

Status codes tell the client what to do next, so pick them by the action they imply. 200 OK returns a result; 201 Created says a new resource exists, with its URL in the Location header; 202 Accepted means the work was queued and will finish later (return a status URL to poll); 204 No Content succeeds with no body. The 4xx codes mean the client must change something before trying again: 400 for a malformed request, 401 Unauthorized when credentials are missing or invalid (despite the name, it is about authentication), 403 Forbidden when the caller is known but not allowed, 404 when the resource doesn't exist (or when you don't want to reveal that it does), 405 for a method the resource doesn't support, 409 Conflict when the request clashes with the current state (a username already taken, an edit based on an old version), 412 Precondition Failed when an If-Match check fails, 422 when the JSON is well formed but breaks a business rule, and 429 Too Many Requests for rate limits. The 5xx codes mean the server failed and the same request might work later: 500 for a bug, 502 and 504 when an upstream server failed or timed out, 503 when the service is overloaded or down for maintenance, ideally with a Retry-After header. Returning 200 with {"error": ...} in the body breaks every client, proxy and dashboard that counts errors by status code.

Headers carry the rest of the contract. Content-Type says what the body is (application/json), Accept says what the client wants back, and Authorization carries credentials. Caching uses Cache-Control and ETag: an ETag is a version tag for a representation, and a client that sends If-None-Match with it gets 304 Not Modified and no body when nothing changed. The same tag prevents lost updates: two people load order 42 at version "v7", both edit, and both send PUT with If-Match: "v7". The first succeeds and moves the order to "v8"; the second gets 412 and must reload instead of silently overwriting the first edit. That is optimistic concurrency, done with plain HTTP.

Strict REST also includes HATEOAS (hypermedia as the engine of application state): responses carry links to the actions now available, so clients follow links rather than building URLs. Few public APIs go that far, and interviewers rarely expect it; consistent resource names, correct methods and honest status codes are what they look for. The widget has three parts: send each method twice and watch what happens to the server's state, pick the right status code for eight situations, and choose the better of two endpoint designs.
